money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The currency is the Danish Krone (DKK). If you travel between Denmark and any non-EU country, you must declare cash of over 10,000 euros (or equivalent). This covers all forms of currency, not only cash. If you don't declare or give the wrong information on entry or exit, you'll need to pay a fine. You don't need to declare cash if you're travelling to or from another EU country. ATMs are common, and credit cards are accepted in most places. Check if your credit card has 'chip and PIN' technology. Many hotels, restaurants and shops need this.

laws.rule: It's illegal to wear clothing which covers the face while in a public place. You'll be fined if you don't comply, and the fine increases for repeat offenders. The law applies to both residents and visitors. Penalties for vandalism, such as graffiti, may include fines, jail and/or deportation. Contact the Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority for more information and guidance on registration. Holders of Australian superannuation accounts should seek advice on taxation before moving to Denmark.

visa-preparation.fastest_entry: Visa-free short stays (90 days or less) as part of the Schengen area, in some cases.
visa-preparation.before_departure: Nothing to lodge before travel today: EES registration happens at the border. ETIAS hadn't started on 2026-11-01.
steps: Denmark is in the Schengen area: short stays of 90 days or less can be visa-free in some cases; other purposes or longer stays need a visa before travel.
At the first Schengen border, give fingerprints and a photo for the Entry/Exit System (EES). It's free; nothing is needed before arrival, and sites charging for it are fraudulent.
Carry your passport when crossing borders, including inside Schengen (temporary internal checks are in place in places).
Greenland and the Faroe Islands aren't in Schengen or the EU.

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: EU baseline (EASA): register once as an operator in the state of residence or establishment, recognised across EASA states; Specific-category work in another state needs cross-border acceptance by that state's authority. National register, zone map and visitor rules checked 6 Nov 2026 (see items); footage routes not yet checked.

items.text: Not yet checked: whether the national aviation authority publishes a list of authorised operators.

EU rules (Regulations 2019/947 and 2019/945): operators register in the EASA state where they reside or are established; Specific-category operations need an operational authorisation or a standard-scenario declaration.

An operator registered in another EASA state may fly here; for Specific-category work it first gets the authorisation or STS declaration at home, then the destination authority must confirm the cross-border operation before flying. Rules for operators from outside EASA states: not yet checked.
Not yet checked: national tourism board or film commission media libraries.

Drones over 250 g, or any carrying a sensor, need a registered operator. Trafikstyrelsen guidance and droneregler.dk differ on which site takes the registration, so the registration URL is not recorded.

Trafikstyrelsen (the transport authority) publishes the official drone zone map on droneregler.dk, taken over from Naviair in 2023. Flying in the geographic drone zones (flight-safety-critical, security-critical and Natura 2000 areas) needs an application to Trafikstyrelsen. Natura 2000 zones are shown in green; some apply only in certain seasons such as breeding time. Military areas need permission from the Defence Command, not Trafikstyrelsen.

VisitDenmark's media library page lists photos and videos for press and promotional use, and links to regional media centres (Copenhagen, Aarhus, Odense, Aalborg, Bornholm and others). Material is only for marketing and promoting Denmark as a travel destination; each regional library has its own terms. Registration and aerial footage were not stated.
